transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-04-02 15:00 PDT
Duration: 62 mins
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Cascade CTO), Ben Lowe (Platform Eng), Cara Singh (Security), Evan Moore (Product)

Summary (auto): Walkthrough of parity mapping and next steps to pilot Redwood for production traffic.

[00:00] Lena Park: Hi everyone, thanks for taking the time, we'll kick off in a sec. I'm Lena from Redwood, with Marco our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Aisha Khan: Good, thanks. We really want to see how close we can get on parity and what the lift looks like.
[00:15] Marco Ruiz: Great, we'll start with a quick map — so we took your examples from OpenAI endpoints and Anthropic dialog, and mapped to Redwood's API shapes and some console patterns. There might be a few naming differences but the semantics are the same.
[00:28] Ben Lowe: Quick note — we're heavy on embeddings for search, but also using streaming completions for chat. Latency is a big for us at the 95th pct.
[00:36] Cara Singh: And on our side, security — we need KMS integration, SSO, audit logs, and SOC2 artifacts.
[00:42] Marco Ruiz: Totally. We'll cover the security piece in the demo and follow up with specific docs. On the API side, basic parity is basically one-to-one: prompt/completion map to Redwood text generation, messages map for chat. There are a couple of differences around stop tokens and streaming chunk shape, but nothing blocking.
[00:58] [00:58] Evan Moore: When you say "a couple of differences", can you give a concrete example?
[01:02] Marco Ruiz: Sure. For example, Together's 'safety_score' fields are returned slightly differently — we surface a normalized safety tuple under 'safety.meta' instead of the raw Together key. That means one line change in our adapter.
[01:16] Lena Park: I'll drop the parity workbook after the call so you can see exact key mappings.
[01:22] [01:22] Aisha Khan: Great. Walk us through the console — we want to see routing and rollout patterns because we have multiple models in prod.
[01:28] Marco Ruiz: On screen — switching to Redwood Console. First panel is model catalog. You can pin specific model versions per route, and then in routing you can define a policy — prefer low-latency variants for interactive chat, cost-optimized for batch embeddings.
[01:44] Ben Lowe: How do you handle fallback? If the low-latency model is out of capacity, we can't fail open and drop to a much higher latency.
[01:52] Marco Ruiz: We have automated fallback chains. You can set regional fallback and capacity tier fallback. If a dedicated pool is exhausted, policy can route to hosted or a cheaper quantized variant. Fallback preserves response shape so your client logic doesn't break.
[02:05] Cara Singh: Is there an audit trail for those routing switches? We need reason codes and timestamps for audits.
[02:10] Marco Ruiz: Yes, we log routing decisions and attach metadata in the request traces; console exposes per-request breadcrumbs and an exportable audit log.
[02:18] [02:18] Aisha Khan: Quick question on Dedicated — what's the minimum commit and how does autoscaling work?
[02:24] Lena Park: Min reserved starts at 4 GPUs at present for our dedicated pools, but that can vary by region — we'll confirm exact SKU options in the sheet. Autoscaling can be configured with burst allowances so short spikes route to a shared pool.
[02:36] Ben Lowe: For our case, we might want a mixed strategy — embeddings on hosted to save cost and chat on dedicated to hit latency.
[02:42] Marco Ruiz: That's a common pattern. Also Optimize (our recommendation engine) will analyze your token distributions and suggest batching window sizes and quant profiles to hit target cost/latency.
[02:52] Evan Moore: Do you have any out-of-the-box quantization recommendations for Together models? We saw artifacts online but want to know risk to quality.
[02:59] Marco Ruiz: We run per-model evaluations — for Together and other families we publish quality vs quantization curves. For some of the medium-sized models 8-bit quant gives about 2-3% quality delta on our evals, but huge cost improvement. We'll share the Optimize report for your typical prompt set.
[03:15] [03:15] Cara Singh: SSO and KMS — can your private deployment use our HSM? We have strict key wrap and rotation rules.
[03:22] Lena Park: For Private we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations; in VPC mode customer owns the keys. For hosted, we offer integration with customer KMS via a customer gateway in some regions — we need to validate network constraints.
[03:33] Ben Lowe: Network wise we use VPC peering and have strict egress rules. Is there an on-prem package?
[03:38] Marco Ruiz: Yep, we have an on-prem package that can run air-gapped. It includes our control plane shim for telemetry that you can opt-in or keep internal.
[03:46] [03:46] Aisha Khan: Can you show the rollout UI for canary? We do gradual ramp ups and need automatic rollback on quality regression.
[03:52] Marco Ruiz: Showing canary config — you can specify traffic percentage by route, tie rollouts to eval suites. If quality drops vs baseline, you can auto-rollback. The eval hook calls your prompt set and uses your chosen metrics (exact match, F1, perplexity).
[04:08] Evan Moore: That eval hook — does it run against production traffic or a stored prompt set?
[04:12] Marco Ruiz: It's stored prompt sets for safety and reproducibility, but you can also stream production samples into a sandboxed evaluation runner, we recommend a mixture.
[04:21] [04:21] Ben Lowe: Let's talk about streaming differences — we use chunked tokens and rely on token ids for incremental highlights in UI. Does Redwood keep token ids consistent?
[04:29] Marco Ruiz: Yes we preserve token id sequences for deterministic models; small differences can happen across tokenizer implementations — we recommend using our tokenizer library which matches server-side tokenization.
[04:41] [04:41] Aisha Khan: Are there any breaking changes we should expect for embeddings shape?
[04:44] Marco Ruiz: The vector dimension is the same for model families, but we do surface normalized vectors for some models to make cosine comparability explicit. That might change a line in your ingestion.
[04:59] [04:59] Lena Park: Quick note on pricing and billing — hosted is usage-based; dedicated is reserved capacity with an overage model. We'll put example TCO comparisons for your traffic in the workbook.
[05:10] Cara Singh: For SOC2, can we get an SOC2 report and pen test artifacts?
[05:15] Lena Park: Yes, we provide SOC2 Type II and pen test summary for enterprise customers. We'll send a redacted pack through the security channel.
[05:22] [05:22] Aisha Khan: Cool. Next — let's talk migration steps. What is a typical small pilot?
[05:27] Marco Ruiz: A common pilot: pick 2-3 routes (one chat, one embedding, one rerank), run canonical traffic through Redwood hosted for 1-2 weeks, compare latency, cost, and quality. If it looks good, swap routing for those routes to Redwood Dedicated or Private depending on security.
[05:40] Ben Lowe: How much engineering time do you expect for adapter changes? We have ~6 endpoints and a small orchestrator.
[05:46] Marco Ruiz: With our parity mappings it's usually a handful of adapter changes — often under a week for a small team. We provide the adapter templates and a CLI that rewrites request/response keys automatically in most cases.
[05:58] [05:58] Evan Moore: Have you seen any gotchas?
[06:01] Marco Ruiz: A couple — tokenizer mismatches and stop-sequence semantics. Also, stateful kv-cache semantics need to be validated if you rely on detachable caches; we help you validate with a test harness.
[06:12] [06:12] Lena Park: We'll include those gotchas in the migration playbook.
[06:18] Cara Singh: From a compliance perspective we need data retention settings and the ability to redact logs.
[06:23] Marco Ruiz: We support redaction at ingest, retention TTLs, and per-tenant log export controls. Private deployments give you full control; hosted customers can opt into additional retention controls in the enterprise plan.
[06:34] [06:34] Ben Lowe: Can we run a short bench to compare token cost for our 3 routes?
[06:38] Marco Ruiz: Yes — if you share a slice of prompts and sample qps, we can run a hosted perf run that returns per-token cost and latency percentiles. We usually do 1k-5k synthetic requests to estimate.
[06:49] Lena Park: Action item — we'll run a 1k run and send results.
[06:53] [06:53] Aisha Khan: How does rate limiting and quotas work? We have per-API-key quotas and also per-tenant controls.
[06:59] Marco Ruiz: We support hierarchical rate limits — key-level, route-level, and tenant-level quotas. Console exposes throttle metrics and you can set hard or soft limits.
[07:10] [07:10] Evan Moore: Regarding function calling — we use structured tool responses, any differences?
[07:15] Marco Ruiz: Function-calling is supported; we preserve the call schema and return structured objects. The only difference is some vendor-specific annotations are normalized.
[07:25] Cara Singh: One more security question — do you store raw prompts? We need to ensure PII is never persisted.
[07:31] Marco Ruiz: By default we retain minimal telemetry. You can disable retention and enable ingest-time redaction. For regulated flows we recommend Private or Dedicated with customer-managed logs.
[07:45] [07:45] Ben Lowe: Let's outline the pilot acceptance criteria. For us: 95th latency under 350ms for chat, embedding p50 under 80ms, and no more than 1.5% quality delta on rerank.
[07:58] Lena Park: Noted — we'll use those as the pilot SLOs and plug into the eval hook.
[08:04] Marco Ruiz: Also we'll pin the model version for the pilot so results are stable, and run baseline comparisons against your current OpenAI/Anthropic outputs.
[08:14] [08:14] Aisha Khan: Who should we loop in on our side for a pilot?
[08:18] Aisha Khan: Ben and Cara are the leads; Evan will own product metrics.
[08:22] Evan Moore: I'll create a pilot doc with scenarios.
[08:26] [08:26] Lena Park: Perfect. We'll follow up with the parity workbook, console recording, and an initial perf run.
[08:34] Ben Lowe: Timeline-wise we want pilot kicked off by mid-April if possible.
[08:38] Lena Park: Sounds feasible. We'll aim to have the run and materials to you by next week.
[08:44] [08:44] Cara Singh: One last ask — can you provide network diagram examples for VPC peering and private deployment?
[08:49] Marco Ruiz: Yes, we'll include sample diagrams and network requirements in the follow-up.
[08:55] [08:55] Evan Moore: Any pricing sensitivity we should know? We care about peak vs average cost.
[08:59] Lena Park: We'll include an example TCO with peak/avg buckets — Optimize can simulate cost under different batching and quant profiles.
[09:07] Marco Ruiz: Ok quick demo of the Optimize recommendations — showing token distribution heatmap, recommended batch size 16 for your embedding usage, and a quantization profile that keeps rerank quality under 1.2% delta.
[09:25] [09:25] Ben Lowe: Nice — that helps.
[09:27] Aisha Khan: Any outstanding legal needs for pilot?
[09:31] Lena Park: The pilot typically runs on our standard trial T&Cs; if you need a custom NDA or DPA we can route to legal. We'll also offer a short pilot MSA for dedicated pilots.
[09:42] [09:42] Cara Singh: We'll need DPA and encryption details before moving deeper.
[09:45] Lena Park: Understood — we'll put Cara as the security contact on the pack.
[09:51] Evan Moore: Alright let's recap.
[09:53] Lena Park: Recap: 1) Lena share parity workbook + console recording by 2026-04-06. 2) Marco run 1k hosted perf tests with your seed prompts and send results by 2026-04-09. 3) Cascade to confirm pilot routes and SLOs by 2026-04-07. 4) Security pack to Cara by 2026-04-05.
[10:17] [10:17] Ben Lowe: That all sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[10:20] Aisha Khan: Thanks — appreciate it.
[10:22] Lena Park: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email and slack.
[10:25] [10:25] Call ends

Notes: Transcription sometimes merged speaker labels; some vendor names were transcribed oddly (e.g., "Together" as "Together AI" vs internal shortname). The parity workbook will enumerate exact field mappings and sample adapter code.
